title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
statement: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the kth largest element in the array. Return it as the kth smallest element of the sorted ascending array instead if that is easier to think about.

examples.explanation: Sorted descending: 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. The second largest is 5.
Sorted descending: 6, 5, 5, 4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 1. The fourth largest is 4.

hints.content: You do not need the whole sorted order. You need one element. What structure keeps the k best values so far?
A heap of size k can hold exactly the k largest elements seen so far.
A min-heap of size k makes the smallest of those k the top of the heap, which is exactly the element you would throw away.
The heap is built on the fly, so it never holds more than k + 1 elements. Sorting the whole array is also accepted but costs O(n log n).

pseudocode: return the top of the heap
invariant: After processing any prefix of the input, the heap holds the k largest values of that prefix.
whyThisPattern: The signal is 'kth largest', which means you only ever need k candidates. Keeping them in a min-heap lets you discard the worst candidate in O(log k), which is cheaper than sorting everything and does not reorder the input.
bruteForce: Sort the array descending and read index k - 1: O(n log n) time and it rewrites the input. For n = 100,000 sorting costs roughly 1.7 * 10^6 comparisons, while the heap version costs about n * log k, which is smaller whenever k is much smaller than n.
interviewExplanation: I keep a min-heap of at most k elements while scanning the array, and whenever the heap grows beyond k I remove its smallest element. That guarantees the heap always holds the k largest values seen so far, so the top of the heap after the scan is the kth largest. This gives O(n log k) time and O(k) space.
commonMistakes: Using a max-heap and keeping k elements, which actually finds the kth smallest.
Returning the last element popped from the heap instead of the top.
Removing an element before adding the new one, which is off by one when k equals the array length.

payload.prompt: Heap contains 5, 6 and the new value 4 with k = 2. Which value leaves the heap?
payload.explanation: The min-heap discards its smallest element, which is the one furthest from the top k.

animationSteps.title: Invariant preserved
animationSteps.description: The heap always holds the k best values of the prefix processed so far.
animationSteps.text: After all six numbers the heap holds 5 and 6, which are the two largest values of the array.

animationSteps.title: Top of the heap is the answer
animationSteps.description: With a min-heap of size k, the top is the kth largest value.
animationSteps.text: The top of the min-heap is 5, which is the second largest element of the array.

payload.message: kth largest is 5, found in one pass with a heap of size k.

options: A sorted array and a position
An unsorted array of integers and an integer k
A heap of k elements, already built
breakdown.explanation: An unsorted array plus a rank. The ordering is absent and has to be partly recovered, not read off.

options: The kth largest value in the array
The kth distinct value in the array
The k largest values, as an array
breakdown.explanation: One value at rank k. Duplicates count separately, so this is a question about position in the sorted order, not about distinct entries.

breakdown.prompt: Does the whole array need sorting to answer this?
options: Yes, sorting is the only way
No, you only need enough order to place rank k
Only if k is larger than the array
breakdown.explanation: No. Sorting is one honest answer, but the question only asks about one rank, and partial selection or a bounded heap answers it without paying for a full ordering.
